In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published a short essay whose title has become a proverb. Imagine, he wrote, a pasture open to all. Each herdsman gains the full benefit of adding one more animal to his herd, while the cost of the additional grazing, the degradation of the pasture, is shared among all the herdsmen. A rational herdsman therefore adds animals, and so does every other, until the pasture is ruined. The logic was seductive because it required no assumptions about greed or stupidity, only self-interest and arithmetic, and its prescriptions were equally crisp: either the resource must be divided into private property, so that each owner bears the cost of his own overuse, or it must be taken under the control of the state. The argument was used for decades to justify the enclosure of grazing land, the nationalisation of forests and the privatisation of fisheries.

The political scientist Elinor Ostrom, who shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in economics, spent her career examining what actually happens to shared resources. Her cases included alpine meadows in Switzerland, village forests in Japan, irrigation communities in Spain and the Philippines, and inshore fisheries in several countries. Many of these arrangements had survived for centuries, with the users themselves managing the resource through rules they had devised; the Water Tribunal of Valencia, which still meets weekly outside the cathedral to settle irrigation disputes, is among the oldest continuously operating courts in Europe. What Hardin had described, Ostrom argued, was not a commons at all but an open-access resource, in which no one has the right to exclude others and no rules govern use. A true commons has a defined group of users and a set of rules about who may take what, when and how much. Hardin’s herdsmen were strangers who could not talk to one another or punish a cheat; the herdsmen of a Swiss village knew each other, met regularly, and had enforced written grazing rules for centuries.

From the surviving cases, Ostrom distilled a set of design principles. Successful commons tend to have clearly defined boundaries, so that it is known who belongs to the group of users; rules that fit the local conditions of the resource; arrangements by which most of those affected can take part in changing the rules; monitoring by users themselves, or by agents accountable to them; sanctions that begin small and escalate for repeated offences; cheap and accessible ways of settling disputes; and recognition of the community’s right to organise by outside authorities. For larger systems, she found, such arrangements were typically nested in several layers. The principles say little about the form of ownership. They are about institutions: who may use, who watches, and how rules are made and enforced. That is why her work was received as a refutation of the claim that only privatisation or central control can prevent ruin.

Critics raised several objections. The first is selection: Ostrom studied commons that had endured, and the failed ones, which left fewer records, are underrepresented, so that the principles may describe the survivors rather than explain survival. A further criticism is that commons which thrived in isolation have often broken down when markets opened and the value of the resource rose, since both the temptation to defect and the number of outsiders increase. The second main objection is scale. The cases are mostly small, stable groups of people who know each other, using a resource whose boundaries are visible and whose misuse can be cheaply observed. The atmosphere, the open ocean and the global climate have none of these features, and it is not obvious that rules that work in an alpine village can be extended to eight billion strangers. Ostrom did not claim that they could; she argued for polycentric governance, in which many overlapping centres of authority, from the local to the international, each handle problems at the scale at which they arise. But this is a research agenda, not a solution.

A third objection is about justice. Cooperation among members of a group does not imply that the group’s arrangements are fair. Community rules can entrench local elites, assign the best plots to the powerful, and exclude newcomers or the landless who have no recognised claim. A commons that preserves the pasture while distributing its benefits unequally has solved an ecological problem and perhaps created a social one. The defenders of the model reply that boundaries and exclusion are intrinsic to any commons, and that the fairness of rules is a matter on which the participatory design principles themselves bear: where those affected can change the rules, the worst inequities are more likely to be challenged. This is plausible, but it is a hope rather than a guarantee.

Nor does privatisation, the alternative, guarantee conservation. The economist Colin Clark showed in the 1970s that a sole owner of a resource maximises the present value of its profits, and that if the resource grows more slowly than the rate of return the owner could earn by selling it and investing the proceeds elsewhere, it can be rational to liquidate it. A whale population that reproduces slowly may be worth more dead and converted into money than alive and breeding. Private ownership removes the problem of the herdsmen’s shared cost, but it introduces a different one, the owner’s impatience, which is set by interest rates rather than by ecology. Secure property rights are thus neither necessary nor sufficient for sustainable use.

The lesson that emerges is more modest than either side’s slogans. Hardin’s model remains a good diagnosis of open-access situations, where no one can be excluded and no rules bind. Ostrom’s work is a catalogue of conditions under which users can credibly commit to restraint and detect those who cheat. Neither is a law of nature. The form of ownership matters less than the structure of rules, monitoring and legitimacy that sits on top of it, and a diagnosis that ignores that structure will mistake an institutional failure for a law of human nature.
questions.question: The author’s distinction between an “open-access resource” and a “commons” implies that:
options: A) shared ownership of a resource always leads to its depletion unless the state intervenes to impose limits on individual consumption
B) Hardin’s herdsmen were irrational, since they ignored the evident cost that their additional animals imposed on the pasture as a whole
C) communities that own a resource jointly are exempt from the problems of free-riding that afflict individual owners of private property
D) overuse results from the absence of enforceable rules among users rather than from shared ownership as such
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 2: Hardin described an open-access resource with no right to exclude and no rules; a true commons has a defined group and rules. So the ruin he predicted comes from the lack of rules, not from joint ownership. Hardin’s herdsmen were rational by assumption, and the passage never says commons are exempt from free-riding.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the selection objection to Ostrom’s findings (paragraph 4)?
options: A) Most of the commons Ostrom studied were small and located in mountainous regions with few opportunities for trade with outsiders.
B) A database that included commons which had collapsed showed much higher failure rates among those lacking her design features.
C) Several commons that had lasted for centuries broke down within a generation after markets opened and the value of the resource rose.
D) Ostrom’s design principles were later adopted by international agencies, which applied them to large-scale fisheries with mixed results.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The objection is that only survivors were studied. A dataset that includes failures and still shows the design features predicting survival removes the bias. The other options raise different issues (scale, market pressure, later application) and do not address selection.

questions.question: The author cites Colin Clark’s argument in order to show that:
options: A) private ownership can still lead to depletion where the resource grows more slowly than the return available elsewhere
B) privatisation always destroys the resources it governs, because private owners care only about their short-term profits at any cost
C) whales and other slow-growing species cannot be protected by any system of property rights, whether private, communal or governmental

A school identifies the students who scored lowest on a mathematics test and enrols them in an extra tutoring programme. A month later the same students take a comparable test, and their average score has risen markedly. The headmaster concludes that the programme works. The conclusion is natural and may be right, but the evidence does not establish it, because the way the students were selected guarantees some improvement even if the tutoring did nothing at all. A test score is partly a product of what a student knows and partly a product of chance: how well she slept, which questions happened to come up, whether a guess landed correctly. Among the students with the lowest scores, many will be those who were unlucky as well as those who knew least. On a second test, the luck is redrawn, and those who were unlucky the first time will on average be less unlucky. The group’s average therefore moves towards the average of all students, whatever is done to it.

This phenomenon, regression to the mean, was identified by Francis Galton in the nineteenth century, when he noticed that exceptionally tall parents tended to have children who were taller than average but less tall than themselves. It is not a force acting on individuals but a statistical consequence of selecting cases because they are extreme on a measure that contains an element of chance. Daniel Kahneman recalled an instructor in a flight school who insisted that praise made cadets perform worse and criticism made them perform better: a cadet who had landed unusually well was praised and then landed less well, while one who had landed badly was shouted at and then improved. The instructor had observed a real pattern and inferred a false cause. Exceptionally good and exceptionally bad performances are both partly luck, and the next performance is likely to be closer to normal either way.

The same logic pervades public policy and medicine. Patients tend to seek treatment when their symptoms are at their worst, and many conditions fluctuate, so that a patient who improves after a remedy may simply have been caught at a peak. Road authorities install speed cameras at junctions where accidents have recently been most numerous; the number of accidents at those junctions falls afterwards, and the cameras are credited. But sites chosen because they had an unusual number of accidents in a given period are, by that very selection, likely to have had bad luck, and some of the subsequent fall would have occurred without any camera. Hospital league tables that rank institutions by a single year’s mortality or infection rate are similarly prone: the hospitals at the bottom one year tend to improve the next, and managers who responded with a flurry of reforms are credited. Studies that adjust for this typically find that the naive before-and-after comparison overstates the effect of the cameras. They usually do not find that the effect disappears: correcting for regression reduces the estimate; it does not necessarily erase it.

One reason is that we are storytellers: a narrative in which an intervention is followed by improvement comes to mind at once, whereas “chance averaged out” is abstract and leaves no one to credit. Another is that the selection that creates the effect is invisible after the fact. By the time we compare the groups, we have forgotten that they were chosen because they were extreme. And the people who run programmes have understandable reasons not to look for alternative explanations: those who introduced a programme are rarely eager to discover that it did less than they had believed, and those who funded it prefer to hear that the money was well spent.

If students are to be tutored, a randomly chosen half of the low scorers should be tutored and the other half not; both halves will regress equally, and any extra improvement among the tutored must be due to the tutoring. Where randomisation is impossible, analysts can reduce the problem by choosing cases on the basis of several periods of data rather than the single worst observation, since a long average contains less luck. If scores were determined almost entirely by stable ability, regression would be small, as with a test that measures a well-practised skill; if they were mostly noise, regression would be large. The effect is not constant but depends on how much of the measure is luck.

To be persuasive, the sceptic must show that regression alone would be expected to produce an improvement of about the observed size, which requires an estimate of how reliable the measure is and how extreme the selected cases were. What had been fabricated from above hardened into constraints and became, in time, a resource that those subject to it could use. The distinction between the imposed and the authentic became blurred precisely because the invention was successful, and the descendants of the original rules now defend them as their own.

It follows that the age of a tradition is a poor guide to its legitimacy. A recent tradition can be inclusive and open to revision, and an ancient one can be oppressive and closed. A tradition becomes a burden not because it is new but because it is treated as unchangeable by those who benefit from it. The historian’s task, then, is not to debunk the traditions of others but to make visible the moment of choice that lies behind them, and so to restore to those who live under them the possibility of choosing again.
questions.question: The criticism that the line between genuine and invented traditions is “a difference of degree” rests on the observation that:
options: A) invented traditions are always based on a real historical practice that the inventors have simply decided to revive again
B) all traditions were originally invented by elites, so that no tradition can be said to have arisen from popular demand
C) oral traditions are more reliable than written ones, because they are checked against the memories of many people living
D) traditions regarded as ancient are themselves continually reshaped in each generation
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 4: oral epics are retold differently each generation and religious rites are reinterpreted, so even ‘genuine’ traditions are reshaped. The other options introduce claims (always revived, all by elites, oral more reliable) that the critics are not said to make.

questions.passage:
We tend to assume that traditions are old, and that their authority derives from their age. In 1983 the historians Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger published a collection of essays that unsettled this assumption. Many practices that present themselves as ancient, they argued, are recent and were deliberately created. The elaborate public ritual of the British monarchy, much of it dating from the late nineteenth century, was devised at a time when the crown’s actual political power was shrinking, and the association of particular tartans with particular Highland clans owes more to the romantic revival of the nineteenth century than to medieval custom. Examples could be multiplied: national flags and anthems, civic ceremonies, school rituals and sporting rites are all younger than the people who perform them suppose. Even the Olympic torch relay, which evokes ancient Greece, was introduced only for the Berlin Games of 1936.

Why are traditions invented? Hobsbawm’s answer was that invention is most frequent when rapid social change weakens the older patterns for which traditions had been designed, or when old traditions prove too inflexible to adapt. The industrial revolution, mass politics and the rise of the nation-state all disrupted established ways of life, and rulers and movements alike needed symbols and rituals that would give the new arrangements the look of continuity. A ceremony that appears to link the present to a distant past confers legitimacy, binds strangers into a community and teaches norms of behaviour by repetition. The point is that tradition is not simply inherited but is also a resource, which can be manufactured when it is needed.

The idea is easily misread. To call a tradition invented is not to call it fake or worthless. Every tradition was once new; what distinguishes a tradition from a fashion is repetition across generations and the claim of continuity with the past. A ritual begun in 1880 and performed ever since is a tradition now, with all the emotional weight that implies. What the historian objects to is not the invention but the false claim of antiquity that frequently accompanies it, because that claim does work. It converts a choice into a duty: a practice adopted by people who might have done otherwise is presented as something the ancestors required, and which cannot therefore be changed without disloyalty. Exposing the moment of invention reminds the living that someone once chose, and that they too may choose.

Critics have complained that the contrast between “genuine” and “invented” traditions is too sharp. Even those traditions regarded as authentically ancient are continually reshaped: oral epics are retold differently in each generation, religious rites are reinterpreted to suit new conditions, and customs survive by changing. The difference between a tradition invented in 1880 and one that has evolved for a thousand years is, on this view, a difference of degree rather than of kind. Moreover, practices that look new may be adaptations of older folk customs whose continuity is difficult to document. A second criticism concerns the manner of invention. The early work sometimes suggests that elites manufactured traditions and imposed them on a passive public. But invented traditions succeed only if people take them up, and they do so only if the new practices resonate with existing sentiments and needs. A ritual that finds no response withers, whatever its sponsors intended. The success of an invention is thus evidence not only of manipulation from above but of demand from below.

The uses of invention are not confined to those in power. Nationalist movements have invented traditions of ancient national unity to justify their claims to statehood, but so have minorities and colonised peoples who revive languages, festivals and costumes to assert dignity against a dominant culture that had treated them as backward. The same technique, the construction of a usable past, serves projects that most observers would judge very differently. This is a reason for not treating the invention of tradition as inherently suspect or inherently admirable. What matters, in each case, is what the tradition is used to do, and for whom.

Ranger’s own contribution, on the colonial history of Africa, shows how consequential the process can be. British administrators who needed to govern large populations through local intermediaries codified what they took to be “customary law”. In doing so they often fixed as rigid rules practices that had been flexible and negotiable, and gave chiefs powers that had earlier been checked by custom. These invented “traditions” were then taken up by Africans themselves, who found that the way to win a hearing from the colonial state was to argue in the terms it recognised. What had been fabricated from above hardened into constraints and became, in time, a resource that those subject to it could use. The distinction between the imposed and the authentic became blurred precisely because the invention was successful, and the descendants of the original rules now defend them as their own.

It follows that the age of a tradition is a poor guide to its legitimacy. A recent tradition can be inclusive and open to revision, and an ancient one can be oppressive and closed. A tradition becomes a burden not because it is new but because it is treated as unchangeable by those who benefit from it. The historian’s task, then, is not to debunk the traditions of others but to make visible the moment of choice that lies behind them, and so to restore to those who live under them the possibility of choosing again.
questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author’s final position?
options: A) Invented traditions are illegitimate, since they rest on a false claim of antiquity that deceives those who are bound by them
B) A tradition’s legitimacy depends less on its age than on whether those who live under it can revise it.
C) Old traditions deserve more respect than new ones, because they have survived the test of many generations of use and change
D) Historians should refrain from exposing the origins of traditions, because such exposure weakens the communities that depend on them
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 7: age is ‘a poor guide to legitimacy’; a tradition becomes a burden when treated as unchangeable by those who benefit, and the historian’s task is to restore the possibility of choosing again. The alternatives contradict each of these claims.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Cities are therefore often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside.
2. This difference is known as the urban heat island effect.
3. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night.
4. Planting trees and installing reflective roofs can reduce the effect.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 gives the physical cause, 1 (‘therefore’) states the result, 2 (‘this difference’) names it, and 4 (‘the effect’) offers remedies.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. The jury system is often defended as a safeguard of liberty.
2. Critics reply, however, that common sense can also carry prejudice.
3. Its defenders argue that ordinary citizens bring common sense to the evidence.
4. Reform proposals therefore tend to focus on the instructions given to jurors rather than on abolishing the institution.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 1 introduces the institution, 3 gives the defenders’ argument, 2 (‘however’) the critics’ reply, and 4 (‘therefore’) the resulting reform focus.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Herd immunity arises when enough people are protected that the pathogen can no longer spread easily.
2. On meeting the real pathogen later, the body recognises it and responds quickly.
3. This response prevents the infection from taking hold, or at least from becoming severe.
4. Vaccines train the immune system by presenting it with a harmless version of a pathogen.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 4 states how vaccines work, 2 the later encounter, 3 (‘this response’) the protective result for the individual, and 1 the population-level consequence.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. They move their money into assets, such as gold or foreign currency, that hold their worth.
2. Governments facing such a spiral often impose capital controls, which carry costs of their own.
3. A currency that is expected to lose value tends to be shunned by savers.
4. This flight deprives the domestic banking system of deposits and weakens the currency further.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 introduces the expectation, 1 (‘they’) the savers’ response, 4 (‘this flight’) its consequence, and 2 the government’s response to the resulting spiral.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Search engines have changed what it means to know something.
2. Whether this is a loss or merely an adaptation remains an open question.
3. Some psychologists therefore argue that people remember where to find information rather than the information itself.
4. Facts that once had to be memorised can now be retrieved in seconds.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 1 states the claim, 4 gives the reason, 3 (‘therefore’) the psychologists’ inference, and 2 (‘this’) the open evaluative question.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'A hospital reports that its overall survival rate is lower than a rival’s, yet when patients are divided into mild and severe cases, it has the higher survival rate in each category. The paradox arises because the first hospital treats a far larger share of severe cases, which have lower survival rates whichever hospital treats them. The lesson is that an aggregate comparison can reverse a comparison within groups when the groups differ in composition, so conclusions depend on whether the data are properly stratified.'
options: A) Aggregate figures can reverse the within-group picture when groups differ in composition, so case mix must be accounted for.
B) The first hospital is in fact worse than its rival, since an overall survival rate is the only fair measure of the quality of care provided.
C) Severe cases have lower survival rates at the first hospital than at its rival, which explains why its overall rate is lower than the rival’s.
D) Survival statistics are meaningless because hospitals can always change the way in which they classify patients as mild or severe in the data.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph describes Simpson’s paradox: the overall comparison reverses within groups because the hospitals’ case mix differs. The other options reverse the hospital’s within-group performance or dismiss statistics altogether.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Cities raise productivity because proximity lets firms share suppliers, workers and ideas. Yet the same density that creates these benefits also produces congestion and high land prices, which push some activity outward. Economists therefore describe the size of a city as a balance between agglomeration economies and congestion costs, a balance that shifts with technology, such as remote work.'
options: A) Cities raise productivity only because firms share suppliers, so congestion and high land prices are of no concern to economists who study them.
B) Remote work has ended the productivity advantage of cities and will cause large cities to disappear within a few decades in all of the countries.
C) City size balances the productivity gains of density against its congestion and rent costs, a balance technology can shift.
D) Congestion and high land prices show that agglomeration economies are an illusion, since the benefits of density are always cancelled by its costs.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph presents city size as a balance of two opposing forces that technology can shift. The distractors drop the costs, overstate remote work, or claim the costs always cancel the benefits.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Herbert Simon argued that real decision-makers rarely maximise: faced with limited time and information, they search until they find an option that is good enough, a strategy he called satisficing. Far from being irrational, this may be the best policy where the cost of further search exceeds its expected gain, though it can lock in mediocre choices when aspirations are set too low.'
options: A) Real decision-makers are irrational because they stop searching before they have found the best available option in the market.
B) Because search is costly, people often settle for good-enough options, which is sensible unless aspirations are set too low.
C) People should always continue to search until they have found the best option, since settling for less is a failure of reason.
D) Satisficing locks in mediocre choices in every case, because aspirations are invariably set too low by people who face time limits.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph defends satisficing as sensible when search is costly, with a caveat about low aspirations. The distractors call it irrational, demand endless search, or claim it always fails.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Inflation-targeting central banks often say that they look through temporary price shocks, such as a sudden rise in vegetable prices. The reasoning is that such shocks fade without policy action, whereas tightening policy in response would depress output with a lag. This reasoning breaks down, however, if the shock persists long enough that ________.'
options: A) the central bank is forced to raise interest rates by less than it would have done in the absence of the shock to prices
B) vegetable prices fall back to their earlier level, restoring the original rate of inflation in the economy as a whole again
C) output rises above its potential level, which makes policy tightening unnecessary until the effects of the shock have faded
D) households and firms begin to expect higher inflation and build it into wages and prices
questions.explanation: Explanation: Looking through is safe only if the shock is temporary. If it persists, expectations adjust and second-round effects on wages and prices make the inflation self-sustaining. The other options describe outcomes consistent with, or irrelevant to, the looking-through logic.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Many online platforms offer a service free of charge in exchange for users’ attention and data. Economists note that when a service is free, the relevant cost to the user is no longer money but ________.'
options: A) the quality of the service, which is necessarily lower than that of any service for which the user pays directly with money
B) the profit of the platform, which must be repaid by the user in the form of higher prices in other markets for goods
C) the attention and personal information surrendered in exchange for access
D) the time spent searching for alternative services, which is always greater than the time spent using the free one itself
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph has just said the exchange is for attention and data, so these are the user’s real costs. The distractors assert unsupported claims about quality, cross-subsidy or search time.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'SAGACIOUS':
options: A) Shrewd
B) Gullible
C) Naive
D) Reticent
questions.explanation: Explanation: Sagacious means having or showing good judgement and wisdom; 'shrewd' is closest. 'Gullible' and 'naive' are opposites.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'MUNIFICENT':
options: A) Generous
B) Miserly
C) Lavish
D) Bountiful
questions.explanation: Explanation: Munificent means very generous; 'miserly' is the antonym. The other options are synonyms.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'INDEFATIGABLE':
options: A) Lethargic
B) Frail
C) Languid
D) Tireless
questions.explanation: Explanation: Indefatigable means never tiring; 'tireless' matches. The others mean lacking energy.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'AUSPICIOUS':
options: A) Promising
B) Fortunate
C) Ominous
D) Propitious
questions.explanation: Explanation: Auspicious means favourable or promising; 'ominous' (suggesting something bad will happen) is the antonym.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'CIRCUMSPECT':
options: A) Wary
B) Impetuous
C) Brazen
D) Reckless
questions.explanation: Explanation: Circumspect means cautious, careful to consider all circumstances before acting; 'wary' is closest. The others are opposites.

questions.question:
Choose the correct word to fill in the blank:
'The politician’s ________ denial, delivered without a flicker of embarrassment, convinced no one.'
options: A) diffident
B) tentative
C) bashful
D) brazen
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Brazen' means bold and shameless, matching a denial delivered without embarrassment. The others suggest shyness or hesitation.

questions.question:
Choose the pair that best fills the blanks:
'The scientist was ________ in her claims, careful never to say more than the data ________.'
options: A) extravagant; justified
B) measured; warranted
C) tentative; contradicted
D) dogmatic; permitted
questions.explanation: Explanation: A scientist who is careful not to say more than the data warrant is 'measured'. The other pairs are contradictory or illogical.

questions.question:
Choose the correct idiom meaning:
'To rest on one’s laurels' means to:
options: A) celebrate a victory with a public display of pride
B) surrender after a long and exhausting struggle
C) rely on past success without further effort
D) refuse to accept a prize that one has earned
questions.explanation: Explanation: Laurels were the traditional symbol of victory; resting on them means relying on past achievements rather than striving further.

questions.question: Select the sentence in which the word 'ENORMITY' is used correctly (in its standard sense):
options: A) The enormity of the crime shocked the entire nation.
B) The enormity of the stadium impressed all the visitors who arrived.
C) She was daunted by the enormity of the mountain range ahead.
D) The enormity of the crowd made it hard to move through the street.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In its standard sense 'enormity' means extreme wickedness, not mere size. Only the crime sentence uses it that way.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'Mathematics ________ my favourite subject at school.'
options: A) are
B) is
C) were
D) have been
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Mathematics' is singular in form and meaning, so it takes 'is'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the following sentence:
'No sooner had he reached (A) / the station than (B) / the train had left (C) / without him (D).'
options: A) No sooner had he reached
B) the station than
C) the train had left
D) without him
questions.explanation: Explanation: After 'No sooner had... than', the second clause takes the simple past: 'than the train left without him'.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) She laid on the sofa all afternoon yesterday.
B) She has laid on the sofa all afternoon today.
C) She lain on the sofa all afternoon yesterday.
D) She lay on the sofa all afternoon.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The intransitive verb 'lie' has the past form 'lay'. 'Laid' (from 'lay') needs an object; 'lain' needs an auxiliary.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'Had the manager been informed earlier, the loss ________ avoided.'
options: A) could be having been
B) can have been
C) could have been
D) could have being
questions.explanation: Explanation: A past unreal condition ('Had... been informed') takes 'could/would have + past participle' in the main clause.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) Each of the boys have finished their homework already.
B) Each of the boys has finished his homework.
C) Each of the boys are finished with his homework.
D) Each of the boys were finishing his homework.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Each' takes a singular verb and pronoun: 'has... his'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the sentence:
'If he would have (A) / told me earlier, (B) / I could have (C) / helped him (D).'
options: A) If he would have
B) told me earlier,
C) I could have
D) helped him
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Would have' is not used in the if-clause of a past conditional: 'If he had told me earlier...'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
'He was deprived ________ his legal rights.'
options: A) from
B) for
C) with
D) of
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Deprive' takes 'of': 'deprived of his rights'.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT sentence:
options: A) Me and my friend went to the market yesterday.
B) My friend and I went to the market yesterday morning.
C) He gave the book to her and me after the lecture.
D) It was she who called the police to the scene.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Subject pronouns are required: 'My friend and I went'. The other sentences use the correct cases.
